Executive Overview

American Express produced a long-term adjusted closing-price increase from $1.2242 on 1972-06-01 to $305.99 on 2026-03-11. On the dataset's adjusted price basis, that equals a 24,894.9% cumulative price return and a 10.81% compounded annual growth rate across 53.8 years.

Investor read-through: AXP's five-decade record is strongly positive, but not smooth. The worst peak-to-trough loss was -83.9%, from $49.30 on 2007-07-19 to $7.93 on 2009-03-06; that drawdown recovered by 2012-04-27. This history supports a long-horizon holding case while underscoring material cyclical risk.
Return profile. The strongest decade by price return was the 1990s at 597.4%, while the weakest was the 1970s at -40.3%.
Risk profile. Full-period annualized volatility was 34.7%. The highest-volatility decade was the 2000s at 43.8%.

Long-Term Price Trend Analysis

The long-term trend is best read on a logarithmic scale because the share price spans more than two orders of magnitude. The chart highlights the central investment pattern: extended compounding phases repeatedly interrupted by deep cyclical drawdowns, especially during financial-system stress periods.

Red bands mark the four deepest threshold drawdown episodes by peak-to-trough depth. Prices are the dataset's adjusted closing prices.

AXP's all-time low close in the dataset was $0.3761 on 1974-10-03, while the all-time high close was $384.04 on 2025-12-11. The latest close was -20.3% relative to that all-time high.

Breaking the history into investable regimes shows that the full-period CAGR masks substantial variation. The 1990s delivered the strongest compounding phase among decade-length periods, while the 2000s combined negative price performance with the largest drawdown of the full sample.

Volatility & Risk Assessment

Daily return volatility annualized to 34.7% over the full sample. The worst single daily return was -26.2% on 1987-10-19; the best was 21.9% on 2020-03-24. The drawdown curve below shows that investors had to withstand multiple losses exceeding 20% before recovering to new closing-price highs.

Drawdown is calculated as each daily close divided by the highest prior close minus one.

Trading Volume Analysis

Volume analysis should account for early-data sparsity: 181 rows record zero volume, and the first non-zero volume date is 1973-02-21. Later decades show structurally higher reported liquidity, with volume spikes clustering around high-volatility periods and major repricing events.

Annual average and median daily volume are computed directly from the Volume column; early zero-volume records are retained rather than imputed.

Methodology and Data Integrity

  • Source All calculations use only /app/benchmark/data.csv; no market prices, dividends, or split values were estimated externally.
  • Returns Price returns use the Close column. CAGR uses calendar time between first and last available trading dates.
  • Volatility Annualized volatility is the sample standard deviation of daily close-to-close returns multiplied by √252.
  • Drawdown Maximum drawdown is computed from the running maximum of adjusted closing prices.
  • Dividends Total dividends paid per share is the sum of the Dividends column; dividend-event yield uses dividend divided by same-day Close.
  • Limitations Early OHLC and volume records are sparse per the dataset documentation; zero volume values are left unchanged and explicitly noted.
Report generated as a self-contained HTML file with embedded SVG charts. Dataset columns: Date, Open, High, Low, Close, Volume, Dividends, Stock Splits.
